accuracy.evidence: Bullying is defined as repeated, intentional hurt where there is an imbalance of power, which matches the Anti-Bullying Alliance definition and UK government guidance (Preventing and tackling bullying). Cyberbullying is that behaviour online. Bystander, upstander, consent, integrity, rights paired with responsibilities, dilemma and digital citizenship use standard primary PSHE meanings, and the safe-action advice (tell a trusted adult, save, block, report) follows NSPCC and Childnet guidance, and the ABA's own example separates a fall-out between equals from bullying.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips teachers report: every mean moment is bullying (prediction 1, the Mia and Leah story, mastery m1), a bystander is not involved (prediction 2, the walk-past spot), an upstander must fight (scene feedback and m8 say you never have to), a right means you can do anything (prediction 4 and the tipping scale), and 'nobody will find out' as a moral reason (the decoy rope card pulls the wrong way).

lab_distinct.evidence: Five mechanisms built for this vocabulary: three yes/no switches that test each story against the three parts of the bullying definition, a draggable You token in a playground scene, a peer-pressure tug rope moved by reason cards with decoys, a rights balance scale that tips on a wrong pairing, and a phone post with tappable problem parts. The distinctness gate passed against all other labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each scene makes the learner apply one definition rather than read it: the verdict fails and names the wrong switch until all three parts match; the upstander task needs both safe actions; the rope only reaches your side with consent, empathy or integrity reasons; each right must find the responsibility that protects it; the post is done only when it is safe, kind and fair.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions come before the matching task and each is answered by it: whether a one-off fall-out is bullying (switch story 2), what someone who walks past is (scene), which reason shows integrity (rope cards) and what responsibility goes with free speech (scale). The reveal quotes the learner's own choice back with spot on or a correction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eleven scenario questions with three word choices drawn from the lesson. A wrong choice gets a targeted line for the common bullying versus fall-out and bystander versus upstander mix-ups, and otherwise the definition of the word picked plus the right answer. The canvas then shows the correct word and its meaning, with a streak counter.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation paragraphs use short sentences with one new word each and concrete school examples (snack, playground, game chat, a photo of a friend). The automatic readability gate passed for learner kid and adult text, and the lab strings stay at a similar level, for example 'Telling is not telling tales.'

no_filler.evidence: Every paragraph introduces or applies one of the twelve target words with an example. There are no stock openers, and the content gate found no banned filler words. The adult text goes straight to what the lab does, the common mistakes and one concrete home routine: save, block and tell.

mobile.evidence: Checked in screenshots on iPhone 13 and desktop. On narrow screens the cards switch to a single column, scene labels wrap inside their boxes, the scale pans are clamped inside the canvas, switches are full-width 46px rows, and every canvas action has a matching button below. No horizontal scroll was seen.

accessibility.evidence: axe passes in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone. Every tap or drag on the canvas has an equivalent text button. The canvas aria-label is updated with the current story and switch states, the rope position or the scale count, and the challenge uses real buttons with polite live feedback.
